claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons modulate how organisms process and respond to environmental stimuli through impacts on arousal, attention, and memory.
source: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons modulate how organisms process and respond to environmental stimuli through impacts on arousal, attention, and memory.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about basal forebrain cholinergic function.

claim: Cholinergic neurons are active during behavioral responding for a reward, even prior to reward delivery and in the absence of discrete stimuli.
source: Using fluorescent imaging, we found that cholinergic neurons are active during behavioral responding for a reward – even prior to reward delivery and in the absence of discrete stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescent imaging data presented in the manuscript (GCaMP photometry experiments shown in Figure 3).

claim: Photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons selectively promoted conditioned responding (licking), but not unconditioned behavior nor innate motor outputs.
source: Photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, or their terminals in the basolateral amygdala (BLA), selectively promoted conditioned responding (licking), but not unconditioned behavior nor innate motor outputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic manipulation experiments shown in Figures 1 and 5, and control experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic terminals in the BLA selectively promoted conditioned responding (licking), but not unconditioned behavior nor innate motor outputs.
source: Photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, or their terminals in the basolateral amygdala (BLA), selectively promoted conditioned responding (licking), but not unconditioned behavior nor innate motor outputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from terminal-specific optogenetic manipulation shown in Figure 5.

claim: In vivo electrophysiological recordings during cholinergic photostimulation revealed reward-contingency-dependent suppression of BLA neural activity.
source: In vivo electrophysiological recordings during cholinergic photostimulation revealed reward-contingency-dependent suppression of BLA neural activity, but not prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data presented in Figure 6.

claim: In vivo electrophysiological recordings during cholinergic photostimulation did not reveal reward-contingency-dependent suppression of prefrontal cortex neural activity.
source: In vivo electrophysiological recordings during cholinergic photostimulation revealed reward-contingency-dependent suppression of BLA neural activity, but not prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Photostimulation of cholinergic terminals suppressed BLA projection neuron activity via monosynaptic muscarinic receptor signaling.
source: Finally, ex vivo experiments demonstrated that photostimulation of cholinergic terminals suppressed BLA projection neuron activity via monosynaptic muscarinic receptor signaling, while also facilitating firing in BLA GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Photostimulation of cholinergic terminals facilitated firing in BLA GABAergic interneurons.
source: Finally, ex vivo experiments demonstrated that photostimulation of cholinergic terminals suppressed BLA projection neuron activity via monosynaptic muscarinic receptor signaling, while also facilitating firing in BLA GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The neural and behavioral effects of basal forebrain cholinergic activation are modulated by reward contingency in a target-specific manner.
source: Taken together, we show that the neural and behavioral effects of basal forebrain cholinergic activation are modulated by reward contingency in a target-specific manner.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating findings from multiple experiments (Figures 1, 5, 6, 7) showing differential effects based on reward contingency.

claim: Most work on basal forebrain cholinergic circuits has focused on how ACh modifies the processing of other stimuli.
source: Most work on basal forebrain cholinergic circuits to date has focused on how ACh modifies the processing of other stimuli, either by increasing attention to conditioned stimuli (Bakin and Weinberger, 1996; Baxter and Chiba, 1999; Gritton et al., 2016; Pinto et al., 2013) or by enhancing associations between conditioned stimuli and unconditioned stimuli/reinforcers in learning and memory (Ballinger et al., 2016; Crouse et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2016; Letzkus et al., 2011; Sturgill et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ACh increases attention to conditioned stimuli.
source: Most work on basal forebrain cholinergic circuits to date has focused on how ACh modifies the processing of other stimuli, either by increasing attention to conditioned stimuli (Bakin and Weinberger, 1996; Baxter and Chiba, 1999; Gritton et al., 2016; Pinto et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: ACh enhances associations between conditioned stimuli and unconditioned stimuli/reinforcers in learning and memory.
source: Most work on basal forebrain cholinergic circuits to date has focused on how ACh modifies the processing of other stimuli, either by increasing attention to conditioned stimuli (Bakin and Weinberger, 1996; Baxter and Chiba, 1999; Gritton et al., 2016; Pinto et al., 2013) or by enhancing associations between conditioned stimuli and unconditioned stimuli/reinforcers in learning and memory (Ballinger et al., 2016; Crouse et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2016; Letzkus et al., 2011; Sturgill et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Less work has been done to explore the behavioral effects of basal forebrain cholinergic neuron activation in the absence of external stimuli.
source: In contrast, less work has been done to explore the behavioral effects of basal forebrain cholinergic neuron activation in the absence of external stimuli (Aitta-Aho et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic projections have considerable physiological effects on postsynaptic neurons ex vivo.
source: Basal forebrain cholinergic projections have considerable physiological effects on postsynaptic neurons ex vivo, where sensory stimuli cannot be presented (Kalmbach et al., 2012; Venkatesan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic projections have prominent direct effects on limbic circuits, including the basolateral amygdala (BLA).
source: Basal forebrain cholinergic projections have prominent direct effects on limbic circuits (Venkatesan et al., 2020), including the basolateral amygdala (BLA) (McDonald and Mascagni, 2011; McDonald and Mascagni, 2010; Unal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Ex vivo optogenetic activation of the cholinergic projection to the BLA suppresses neural activity at low firing rates.
source: Ex vivo optogenetic activation of the cholinergic projection to the BLA affects postsynaptic activity differentially, suppressing neural activity at low firing rates (Unal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: In vivo cholinergic activation may increase spontaneous BLA neural firing.
source: In contrast, however, in vivo cholinergic activation may increase spontaneous BLA neural firing (Jiang et al., 2016), suggesting that the postsynaptic effects of basal forebrain cholinergic projections may be depend upon as yet unidentified influences.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study and represents a contrast to ex vivo findings.

claim: The postsynaptic effects of basal forebrain cholinergic projections may depend upon as yet unidentified influences.
source: In contrast, however, in vivo cholinergic activation may increase spontaneous BLA neural firing (Jiang et al., 2016), suggesting that the postsynaptic effects of basal forebrain cholinergic projections may be depend upon as yet unidentified influences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the contrast between ex vivo and in vivo findings cited in the text.

claim: During WoOT, rewards were only delivered if mice licked the spout during an unsignaled Window of Opportunity.
source: Rewards were only delivered if mice licked the spout during an unsignaled Window of Opportunity.
evidence: This describes the task design used in the experiments.

claim: Because windows were not discretely cued and occurred with variable ITIs, mice did not know whether any given lick would be rewarded.
source: Because rewards were only delivered after the first lick in a Window of Opportunity, and because windows were not discretely cued and occurred with variable ITIs, mice did not know whether any given lick would be rewarded.
evidence: This is an inference about the task design and what mice could predict.

claim: The underlying task structure of WoOT is an operant, variable-interval reinforcement schedule with limited hold.
source: The underlying task structure of this task is an operant, variable-interval reinforcement schedule with limited hold (Ferster and Skinner, 1957).
evidence: This characterizes the task structure with reference to established operant conditioning terminology.

claim: Training mice in WoOT conditioned them to lick the spout with a relatively stable pattern of intermittent lick bouts.
source: Training mice in this manner conditioned them to lick the spout with a relatively stable pattern of intermittent lick bouts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nearly 90% of neurons expressing ChR2 were cholinergic, as confirmed by immunostaining for choline acetyltransferase (ChAT).
source: Nearly 90% of neurons expressing ChR2 were cholinergic, as confirmed by immunostaining for choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), an obligate enzyme in the synthesis of ACh (Prado et al., 2002 Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: ChAT is an obligate enzyme in the synthesis of ACh.
source: Nearly 90% of neurons expressing ChR2 were cholinergic, as confirmed by immunostaining for choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), an obligate enzyme in the synthesis of ACh (Prado et al., 2002 Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ChAT function, supported by a citation.

claim: Both ChR2 and eYFP mice were similarly likely to lick at least once on an unsignaled Window of Opportunity as on an Unrewarded Window prior to photostimulation.
source: During early WoOT training, which did not yet involve photostimulation, mice were trained for a mean of seven sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and both ChR2 and eYFP mice were similarly likely to lick at least once on an unsignaled Window of Opportunity as on an Unrewarded Window, confirming that mice could not predict reward delivery prior to licking, and that viral expression in the absence of photostimulation did not influence behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mice could not predict reward delivery prior to licking during early WoOT training.
source: During early WoOT training, which did not yet involve photostimulation, mice were trained for a mean of seven sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and both ChR2 and eYFP mice were similarly likely to lick at least once on an unsignaled Window of Opportunity as on an Unrewarded Window, confirming that mice could not predict reward delivery prior to licking, and that viral expression in the absence of photostimulation did not influence behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data showing similar licking on rewarded and unrewarded windows.

claim: Viral expression in the absence of photostimulation did not influence behavior.
source: During early WoOT training, which did not yet involve photostimulation, mice were trained for a mean of seven sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and both ChR2 and eYFP mice were similarly likely to lick at least once on an unsignaled Window of Opportunity as on an Unrewarded Window, confirming that mice could not predict reward delivery prior to licking, and that viral expression in the absence of photostimulation did not influence behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of difference between ChR2 and eYFP groups prior to photostimulation.

claim: Prior to photostimulation, ChR2 and eYFP groups collected similar numbers of rewards.
source: Prior to photostimulation, ChR2 and eYFP groups also collected similar numbers of rewards (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), had similar lick rates over entire sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), and had similar lick bout characteristics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I), suggesting a stable setting in which to study the effects of transient photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Prior to photostimulation, ChR2 and eYFP groups had similar lick rates over entire sessions.
source: Prior to photostimulation, ChR2 and eYFP groups also collected similar numbers of rewards (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), had similar lick rates over entire sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), and had similar lick bout characteristics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I), suggesting a stable setting in which to study the effects of transient photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Prior to photostimulation, ChR2 and eYFP groups had similar lick bout characteristics.
source: Prior to photostimulation, ChR2 and eYFP groups also collected similar numbers of rewards (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), had similar lick rates over entire sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), and had similar lick bout characteristics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I), suggesting a stable setting in which to study the effects of transient photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: In Photostim-Unreinforced sessions, licking did not increase during photostimulated windows compared to windows with no photostimulation, in either ChR2 or eYFP mice.
source: In these Photostim-Unreinforced sessions, licking did not increase during photostimulated windows compared to windows with no photostimulation, in either ChR2 or eYFP mice (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In Photostim-Reinforced sessions, photostimulation increased licking in mice expressing ChR2, but not eYFP.
source: However, in these Photostim-Reinforced sessions, photostimulation increased licking in mice expressing ChR2, but not eYFP (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: During windows with no photostimulation, licking remained similar between ChR2 and eYFP mice.
source: In contrast, during windows with no photostimulation, licking remained similar between ChR2 and eYFP mice (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Transient photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons became capable of promoting an operant conditioned response, increasing the likelihood and decreasing the latency of licking, but only after being paired with the opportunity to collect rewards.
source: Transient photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons became capable of promoting an operant conditioned response, increasing the likelihood and decreasing the latency of licking, but only after being paired with the opportunity to collect rewards.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating findings from Figure 1H and 1I.

claim: Even a single 5 ms laser pulse was sufficient both to increase the likelihood of licking and accelerate the latency of the first lick following photostimulation onset.
source: Even a single 5 ms laser pulse was sufficient both to increase the likelihood of licking (Figure 1J) and accelerate the latency of the first lick following photostimulation onset (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1J and 1K.

claim: Brief photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons can promote conditioned responding when paired with potential reinforcement.
source: In summary, brief photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons can promote conditioned responding when paired with potential reinforcement.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating findings from Figure 1J and 1K.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic photostimulation did not increase locomotion in an open-field test.
source: Basal forebrain cholinergic photostimulation did not increase locomotion in an open-field test (OFT, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B), as measured by mouse velocity (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Photostimulation did not modify innate location preference in an open-field test.
source: Additionally, photostimulation did not modify innate location preference, as measured by the amount of time spent in the center of the open field, which was avoided similarly by ChR2 and eYFP mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Neither ChR2 nor eYFP mice demonstrated a preference for the side paired with photostimulation in a real-time place preference assay.
source: Neither ChR2 nor eYFP mice demonstrated a preference for the side paired with photostimulation, suggesting that photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons was not inherently reinforcing (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4F.

claim: Photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons was not inherently reinforcing.
source: Neither ChR2 nor eYFP mice demonstrated a preference for the side paired with photostimulation, suggesting that photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons was not inherently reinforcing (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of place preference in the RTPP assay.

claim: There was no difference in locomotion around the time of photostimulation between ChR2 and eYFP mice during either Photostim-Unreinforced or Photostim-Reinforced sessions.
source: There was no difference in locomotion around the time of photostimulation between ChR2 and eYFP mice during either Photostim-Unreinforced or Photostim-Reinforced sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by treadmill locomotion data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4G.

claim: Locomotion did not differ significantly between Photostim-Unreinforced and Photostim-Reinforced sessions for either ChR2 or eYFP mice.
source: Locomotion also did not differ significantly between Photostim-Unreinforced and Photostim-Reinforced sessions for either ChR2 or eYFP mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by treadmill locomotion data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4H.

claim: During Photostim-Unreinforced sessions, photostimulation of cholinergic neurons caused a modest increase in pupil dilation in ChR2 mice compared to eYFP mice.
source: During Photostim-Unreinforced sessions, photostimulation of cholinergic neurons caused a modest increase in pupil dilation in ChR2 mice compared to eYFP mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4I, left; rank-sum between groups, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by pupillometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4I.

claim: The first significant difference in pupil size between ChR2 and eYFP mice began 1.2 s after laser onset during Photostim-Unreinforced sessions.
source: The first significant difference in pupil size between ChR2 and eYFP mice began 1.2 s after laser onset.
evidence: This claim is supported by pupillometry data analysis.

claim: During Photostim-Reinforced sessions, photostimulation caused an increase in pupil dilation in ChR2 mice compared to eYFP mice, beginning 0.7 s after laser onset.
source: During Photostim-Reinforced sessions, photostimulation also caused an increase in pupil dilation in ChR2 mice compared to eYFP mice, now beginning 0.7 s after laser onset (Figure 1—figure supplement 4I, right; rank-sum between groups, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by pupillometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4I.

claim: Pupil changes were larger during Photostim-Reinforced than Photostim-Unreinforced sessions for ChR2 mice.
source: Pupil changes were larger during Photostim-Reinforced than Photostim-Unreinforced sessions for ChR2 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by pupillometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4J.

claim: There was no clear change in pupil size after photostimulation for eYFP mice.
source: There was no clear change in pupil size after photostimulation for eYFP mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by pupillometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4J.

claim: During both Photostim-Unreinforced and Photostim-Reinforced sessions, pupils dilated similarly in ChR2 and eYFP mice following reward delivery.
source: During both sessions, pupils dilated similarly in ChR2 and eYFP mice following reward delivery (Figure 1—figure supplement 4L).
evidence: This claim is supported by pupillometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4L.

claim: Cholinergic photostimulation increases arousal modestly, but this effect becomes evident more slowly for pupillary dilation than for licking behavior.
source: Therefore, cholinergic photostimulation increases arousal modestly, but this effect becomes evident more slowly for pupillary dilation than for licking behavior (0.5 s latency for licking as in Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the timing of pupil dilation and licking responses.

claim: Photostim-induced licking was abolished by systemic muscarinic receptor antagonist administration.
source: Photostim-induced licking was abolished by systemic muscarinic receptor antagonist administration.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ChR2 mice no longer responded more during photostimulation than during Unrewarded Windows after scopolamine 1 mg/kg administration.
source: Scopolamine 1 mg/kg: ChR2 mice no longer responded more during photostimulation than during Unrewarded Windows, and no longer responded more during photostimulation than eYFP mice, although they continued to respond more during tones than intertrial intervals (ITIs).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ChR2 mice continued to respond more during tones than ITIs after scopolamine 1 mg/kg administration.
source: Scopolamine 1 mg/kg: ChR2 mice no longer responded more during photostimulation than during Unrewarded Windows, and no longer responded more during photostimulation than eYFP mice, although they continued to respond more during tones than intertrial intervals (ITIs).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Conditioned responding to tones and photostimulation after injection of the nicotinic receptor antagonist mecamylamine was similar to that after saline control for both ChR2 and eYFP mice.
source: In contrast, conditioned responding to tones and photostimulation after injection of the nicotinic receptor antagonist mecamylamine was similar to that after saline control for both ChR2 and eYFP mice (Figure 2C, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Muscarinic receptors, rather than nicotinic receptors, were necessary for conditioned responding to basal forebrain cholinergic neuron photostimulation.
source: Therefore, muscarinic receptors, rather than nicotinic receptors, were necessary for conditioned responding to basal forebrain cholinergic neuron photostimulation.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating findings from the pharmacology experiments in Figure 2.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons have been described to be active during reinforcer delivery.
source: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons have been described to be active during reinforcer delivery (Hangya et al., 2015), reward consumption (Harrison et al., 2016), movements including locomotion (Harrison et al., 2016; Nelson and Mooney, 2016), and conditioned stimuli (Guo et al., 2019; Parikh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons have been described to be active during reward consumption.
source: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons have been described to be active during reinforcer delivery (Hangya et al., 2015), reward consumption (Harrison et al., 2016), movements including locomotion (Harrison et al., 2016; Nelson and Mooney, 2016), and conditioned stimuli (Guo et al., 2019; Parikh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons have been described to be active during movements including locomotion.
source: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons have been described to be active during reinforcer delivery (Hangya et al., 2015), reward consumption (Harrison et al., 2016), movements including locomotion (Harrison et al., 2016; Nelson and Mooney, 2016), and conditioned stimuli (Guo et al., 2019; Parikh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons have been described to be active during conditioned stimuli.
source: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons have been described to be active during reinforcer delivery (Hangya et al., 2015), reward consumption (Harrison et al., 2016), movements including locomotion (Harrison et al., 2016; Nelson and Mooney, 2016), and conditioned stimuli (Guo et al., 2019; Parikh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons increased conditioned responding independent of conditioned cues, prior to reinforcer delivery or consumption, and without affecting unconditioned movements such as locomotion.
source: However, we observed that photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons increased conditioned responding independent of these factors: in the absence of conditioned cues, prior to reinforcer delivery or consumption, and without affecting unconditioned movements such as locomotion.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating findings from multiple experiments (Figures 1, 1—figure supplement 4).

claim: Fluorescence levels increased at the time of events in the 470 nm wavelength signal channel, but not the 405 reference channel, during the cued task.
source: Fluorescence levels increased at the time of events in the 470 nm wavelength signal channel (blue), but not the 405 reference channel (violet) (tone: t55 = 2.64, #p=0.064; Lick leading to Reward Delivery [Lick & Rwd]: t55 = 7.57, ***p<0.001; Licks in the absence of Cue & Reward Delivery [Lick, No Rwd]: t55 = 5.29, ***p<0.001; Sidak correction for six multiple comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by GCaMP photometry data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Changes in fluorescent activity were observed both at the time of licking that triggered reward delivery and at the time of licking in the absence of reward delivery during WoOT.
source: Even in this context, without discrete tones or cues, changes in fluorescent activity were observed both at the time of licking that triggered reward delivery (Figure 3I), as well as at the time of licking in the absence of reward delivery (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by GCaMP photometry data shown in Figure 3I, J, K.

claim: Cholinergic neurons are physiologically active at the time of conditioned responding, even in the absence of cues and reward consumption.
source: This suggests that cholinergic neurons are physiologically active at the time of conditioned responding, even in the absence of cues and reward consumption.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GCaMP photometry data in Figure 3.

claim: BLA ACh sensor fluorescence levels increased at the time of events in the 470 nm wavelength signal channel, but not the 405 reference channel, during the cued task.
source: Fluorescence levels increased at the time of events in the 470 nm wavelength signal channel (blue), but not the 405 reference channel (violet) (tone: t99 = 2.80, *p=0.036; Lick leading to Reward Delivery [Lick & Rwd]: t99 = 5.49, ***p<0.001; Licks in the absence of Cue & Reward Delivery [Lick, No Rwd]: t99 = 2.91, *p<0.027; Sidak correction for six multiple comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by ACh sensor data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Changes in fluorescent signals were observed both at the time of licking that triggered reward delivery and at the time of licking without subsequent reward delivery during WoOT.
source: Even in this context, without discrete tones or other discrete cues, changes in fluorescent signals were observed both at the time of licking that triggered reward delivery and at the time of licking without subsequent reward delivery (Figure 4J–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by ACh sensor data shown in Figure 4J, K, L.

claim: BLA ACh levels increased at the time of conditioned responding, even in the absence of discrete cues and reward consumption.
source: These results suggest that BLA ACh levels increased at the time of conditioned responding, even in the absence of discrete cues and reward consumption.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ACh sensor data in Figure 4.

claim: Transient photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic terminals in the BLA drove conditioned responding in a temporally precise way, only when photostimulation was associated with the opportunity to collect rewards.
source: Hence, transient photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic terminals in the BLA drove conditioned responding in a temporally precise way, only when photostimulation was associated with the opportunity to collect rewards, similar to results with somatic basal forebrain cholinergic neuron photostimulation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating findings from Figure 5B and comparing to Figure 1.

claim: Photostimulation elicited robust ACh sensor responses in mice expressing ChrimsonR, but not in mice expressing a control fluorophore.
source: Photostimulation elicited robust responses in mice expressing ChrimsonR, but not in mice expressing a control fluorophore (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ACh sensor data during concurrent photostimulation shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The amount of measured ACh fluorescence did not depend upon whether photostimulation was provided in Photostim-Unreinforced or Photostim-Reinforced sessions.
source: The amount of measured fluorescence did not depend upon whether photostimulation was provided in Photostim-Unreinforced or Photostim-Reinforced sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by ACh sensor data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Reward associations may gate postsynaptic responses to photostimulation, rather than presynaptically changing ACh release.
source: Taken together with our previous finding that photostimulation of cholinergic terminals in the BLA selectively elevated licking during Photostim-Reinforced sessions (Figure 5C), our observation that BLA ACh levels did not change with reward suggests that reward associations may gate postsynaptic responses to photostimulation, rather than presynaptically changing ACh release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combination of behavioral and ACh sensor data.

claim: The amount of ACh sensor fluorescence evoked by 1–2 laser pulses was similar to levels of ACh at the time of reward delivery in the absence of any photostimulation.
source: The amount of ACh sensor fluorescence evoked by 1–2 laser pulses, which had been sufficient to promote conditioned responding when photostimulation was targeted to the soma (Figure 1), was similar to levels of ACh at the time of reward delivery in the absence of any photostimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ACh sensor data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A level of optogenetically induced ACh release similar to physiologic release can promote conditioned responding, specifically when paired with the opportunity to collect rewards.
source: Therefore, a level of optogenetically induced ACh release similar to physiologic release can promote conditioned responding, specifically when paired with the opportunity to collect rewards (Photostim-Reinforced sessions).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ACh sensor data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BLA and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) are both involved in conditioned behavior.
source: The BLA and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) are both involved in conditioned behavior (Cardinal et al., 2002), receive projections from basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (Kitt et al., 1994; Woolf et al., 1984), and are functionally interrelated (Burgos-Robles et al., 2017; Likhtik et al., 2014; Likhtik et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The BLA and dmPFC receive projections from basal forebrain cholinergic neurons.
source: The BLA and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) are both involved in conditioned behavior (Cardinal et al., 2002), receive projections from basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (Kitt et al., 1994; Woolf et al., 1984), and are functionally interrelated (Burgos-Robles et al., 2017; Likhtik et al., 2014; Likhtik et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The BLA and dmPFC are functionally interrelated.
source: The BLA and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) are both involved in conditioned behavior (Cardinal et al., 2002), receive projections from basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (Kitt et al., 1994; Woolf et al., 1984), and are functionally interrelated (Burgos-Robles et al., 2017; Likhtik et al., 2014; Likhtik et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: During photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, dmPFC neural activity increased overall across the population.
source: During photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, dmPFC neural activity increased overall across the population (Figure 6B, left; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The increase in dmPFC population neural activity during photostimulation was similar for both Photostim-Unreinforced sessions and Photostim-Reinforced sessions.
source: The increase in dmPFC population neural activity during photostimulation was similar for both Photostim-Unreinforced sessions (purple) and Photostim-Reinforced sessions (green).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The effects of photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons on BLA neural activity differed depending on the session.
source: In contrast to the dmPFC, the effects of photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons on BLA neural activity differed depending on the session (Figure 6B, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In Photostim-Unreinforced sessions, the overall BLA population response consisted of facilitation, particularly at onset.
source: In Photostim-Unreinforced sessions (purple), the overall BLA population response consisted of facilitation, particularly at onset, whereas in the Photostim-Reinforced sessions (green), the BLA population response had a more striking and sustained suppression.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In Photostim-Reinforced sessions, the BLA population response had a more striking and sustained suppression.
source: In Photostim-Unreinforced sessions (purple), the overall BLA population response consisted of facilitation, particularly at onset, whereas in the Photostim-Reinforced sessions (green), the BLA population response had a more striking and sustained suppression.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The difference in the BLA population response between the two sessions was evident as early as 135 ms after photostimulation onset.
source: The difference in the BLA population response between the two sessions was evident as early as 135 ms after photostimulation onset and occurred with even shorter durations of photostimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data analysis.

claim: There were minimal changes related to photostimulation in control mice expressing eYFP for both Photostim-Unreinforced and Paired sessions types.
source: There were minimal changes related to photostimulation in control mice expressing eYFP for both Photostim-Unreinforced and Paired sessions types (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by control in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the dmPFC, the proportion of neurons facilitated and suppressed by photostimulation was stable across session types.
source: In the dmPFC, the proportion of neurons facilitated and suppressed by photostimulation was stable across session types (Figure 6F, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In the BLA, the proportion of individual neurons that were facilitated tended to decreased during Photostim-Reinforced sessions.
source: In the BLA, however, the proportion of individual neurons that were facilitated tended to decreased during Photostim-Reinforced sessions and the proportion of neurons that were suppressed increased during Photostim-Reinforced sessions (Figure 6F, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In the BLA, the proportion of neurons that were suppressed increased during Photostim-Reinforced sessions.
source: In the BLA, however, the proportion of individual neurons that were facilitated tended to decreased during Photostim-Reinforced sessions and the proportion of neurons that were suppressed increased during Photostim-Reinforced sessions (Figure 6F, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: A higher proportion of BLA neurons was suppressed than dmPFC neurons during both session types.
source: Comparing between these regions (Figure 6G), a higher proportion of BLA neurons was suppressed than dmPFC neurons during both session types, but a lower proportion of BLA neurons than dmPFC neurons was facilitated during the Photostim-Reinforced sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: A lower proportion of BLA neurons than dmPFC neurons was facilitated during the Photostim-Reinforced sessions.
source: Comparing between these regions (Figure 6G), a higher proportion of BLA neurons was suppressed than dmPFC neurons during both session types, but a lower proportion of BLA neurons than dmPFC neurons was facilitated during the Photostim-Reinforced sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Cholinergic effects in vivo differ between target regions and depend upon reinforcer context in the amygdala.
source: These findings suggested that cholinergic effects in vivo differ between target regions and depend upon reinforcer context in the amygdala.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating findings from the in vivo electrophysiology experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Neurons in the dmPFC that were facilitated by photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons during the Photostim-Reinforced sessions had higher baseline firing rates than neurons that were suppressed.
source: Neurons in the dmPFC that were facilitated by photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons during the Photostim-Reinforced sessions had higher baseline firing rates than neurons that were suppressed (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: BLA-mPFC neurons responded to cholinergic terminal photostimulation with a prolonged suppression.
source: BLA-mPFC neurons responded to cholinergic terminal photostimulation with a prolonged suppression (Figure 7E and F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7E, F, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: BLAGABA neurons responded to cholinergic photostimulation with a rapid and more transient facilitation.
source: In contrast, BLAGABA neurons responded to cholinergic photostimulation with a rapid and more transient facilitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7E, F.

claim: The amplitude of the fast excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) was greater in BLAGABA neurons compared with BLA-mPFC neurons.
source: The amplitude of the fast excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) was greater in BLAGABA neurons compared with BLA-mPFC neurons, while the inhibitory postsynaptic current (IPSP) amplitude was greater in BLA-mPFC neurons relative to BLAGABA (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The inhibitory postsynaptic current (IPSP) amplitude was greater in BLA-mPFC neurons relative to BLAGABA.
source: The amplitude of the fast excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) was greater in BLAGABA neurons compared with BLA-mPFC neurons, while the inhibitory postsynaptic current (IPSP) amplitude was greater in BLA-mPFC neurons relative to BLAGABA (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Short-latency facilitation in GABAergic neurons and longer-latency suppression in projection neurons represented independent, direct monosynaptic responses to photostimulation of cholinergic afferents.
source: These represented independent, direct monosynaptic responses to photostimulation of cholinergic afferents as each response persisted in the absence of spike-driven synaptic release (to eliminate indirect/polysynaptic transmission), blocked by tetrodotoxin (TTX) (Figure 7H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data with TTX/4AP shown in Figure 7H and I.

claim: Photostimulation-evoked IPSPs in BLA-mPFC neurons were blocked by a muscarinic antagonist, but not nicotinic antagonist.
source: Photostimulation-evoked IPSPs in BLA-mPFC neurons were blocked by a muscarinic antagonist, but not nicotinic antagonist (Figure 7J, top row).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo pharmacology data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The photostimulation-evoked facilitation in BLAGABA neurons was blocked by a nicotinic antagonist, but not a muscarinic antagonist.
source: In contrast, the photostimulation-evoked facilitation in BLAGABA neurons was blocked by a nicotinic antagonist, but not a muscarinic antagonist (Figure 7J, bottom row).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo pharmacology data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Cholinergic afferents suppress BLA output through multiple, molecularly specific pathways, both through direct muscarinic suppression of projection neurons, as well as through nicotinic facilitation of GABAergic neurons.
source: These results suggest a circuit model in which cholinergic afferents suppress BLA output through multiple, molecularly specific pathways, both through direct muscarinic suppression of projection neurons, as well as through nicotinic facilitation of GABAergic neurons, which can locally inhibit BLA projection neurons (Lee and Kim, 2019; Woodruff and Sah, 2007; Figure 7K).
evidence: This is a circuit model inferred from the ex vivo electrophysiology and pharmacology data in Figure 7, combined with citations to prior studies about local inhibition.

claim: GABAergic neurons can locally inhibit BLA projection neurons.
source: These results suggest a circuit model in which cholinergic afferents suppress BLA output through multiple, molecularly specific pathways, both through direct muscarinic suppression of projection neurons, as well as through nicotinic facilitation of GABAergic neurons, which can locally inhibit BLA projection neurons (Lee and Kim, 2019; Woodruff and Sah, 2007; Figure 7K).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The effects of cholinergic input to the BLA appear to be a suppression of BLA projector neuron output.
source: In total, the effects of cholinergic input to the BLA appear to be a suppression of BLA projector neuron output, and this effect may be most prominent when the system is primed to respond to cholinergic input by behavioral reinforcement.
evidence: This is a summary inference integrating findings from the ex vivo experiments in Figure 7 with the in vivo findings in Figure 6.

claim: The suppression of BLA projector neuron output may be most prominent when the system is primed to respond to cholinergic input by behavioral reinforcement.
source: In total, the effects of cholinergic input to the BLA appear to be a suppression of BLA projector neuron output, and this effect may be most prominent when the system is primed to respond to cholinergic input by behavioral reinforcement.
evidence: This is a speculative inference integrating findings from multiple experiments.

claim: Photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons can promote conditioned responding, even in the absence of discrete external cues.
source: Here we demonstrate that photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons can promote conditioned responding, even in the absence of discrete external cues.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the main finding from Figure 1.

claim: ACh has long been posited to play an important role in directing attention to extrinsic stimuli, as measured by facilitating conditioned responses to such stimuli.
source: ACh has long been posited to play an important role in directing attention to extrinsic stimuli, as measured by facilitating conditioned responses to such stimuli (Parikh et al., 2007; Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons only drove conditioned responding when paired with the opportunity to collect rewards.
source: Remarkably, photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons only drove conditioned responding when paired with the opportunity to collect rewards (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary claim of a key finding from Figure 1.

claim: Basal forebrain neurons, including cholinergic neurons, are active at the time of both positively and negatively valenced reinforcers.
source: Basal forebrain neurons, including cholinergic neurons, are active at the time of both positively and negatively valenced reinforcers (Hangya et al., 2015; Harrison et al., 2016; Peck and Salzman, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: At least some part of the previously described reward associations may be due to reward collection behavior such as licking, rather than only reward per se.
source: Our results demonstrate that at least some part of the previously described reward associations may be due to reward collection behavior such as licking, rather than only reward per se.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current findings in the context of prior literature.

claim: Previous work has suggested that ACh may amplify the effects of reinforcers during learning and strengthen plasticity.
source: Previous work has also suggested that ACh may amplify the effects of reinforcers during learning and strengthen plasticity (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Reward availability modified the behavioral and neural effects of basal forebrain cholinergic neuron photostimulation itself.
source: In the current study, reward availability modified the behavioral and neural effects of basal forebrain cholinergic neuron photostimulation itself.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating findings from Figures 1, 5, and 6.

claim: BLA neurons became more suppressed as a population during Photostim-Reinforced sessions, appearing to become more similar to findings in an ex vivo preparation from behaviorally naïve animals.
source: BLA neurons became more suppressed as a population (Figure 6), appearing to become more similar to findings in an ex vivo preparation from behaviorally naïve animals (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing in vivo (Figure 6) and ex vivo (Figure 7) findings.

claim: Effects of ACh may be unmasked or amplified by reward availability.
source: Taken together, these data suggest a model wherein effects of ACh may be unmasked or amplified by reward availability.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the findings.

claim: Cholinergic terminals can express presynaptic receptors, including cholinergic receptors, which may modulate ACh release.
source: Cholinergic terminals can express presynaptic receptors, including cholinergic receptors, which may modulate ACh release (Muller et al., 2016; Thany and Tricoire-Leignel, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Photostimulation of cholinergic terminals in the BLA evoked similar levels of ACh in Photostim-Unreinforced and Photostim-Reinforced sessions.
source: However, photostimulation of cholinergic terminals in the BLA evoked similar levels of ACh in Photostim-Unreinforced and Photostim-Reinforced sessions (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by ACh sensor data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Similar levels of ACh may have been gated or differentially interpreted by downstream, postsynaptic neurons, depending on reward availability.
source: This suggests that the similar levels of ACh instead may have been gated or differentially interpreted by downstream, postsynaptic neurons, depending on reward availability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ACh sensor data in Figure 5.

claim: The postulation of gating may be mediated by coincident signals of reinforcement to the BLA, such as dopaminergic inputs.
source: The postulation of such gating merits future investigation, but may be mediated by coincident signals of reinforcement to the BLA, such as dopaminergic inputs (Lutas et al., 2022; Lutas et al., 2019; Tye et al., 2010), given that dopaminergic receptors are expressed by BLA neurons that also express cholinergic receptors (Równiak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Dopaminergic receptors are expressed by BLA neurons that also express cholinergic receptors.
source: The postulation of such gating merits future investigation, but may be mediated by coincident signals of reinforcement to the BLA, such as dopaminergic inputs (Lutas et al., 2022; Lutas et al., 2019; Tye et al., 2010), given that dopaminergic receptors are expressed by BLA neurons that also express cholinergic receptors (Równiak et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: dmPFC neurons were responsive to photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, but these responses did not appear to be dependent on the association between photostimulation with reward.
source: Although dmPFC neurons were responsive to photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, these responses did not appear to be dependent on the association between photostimulation with reward, despite the robust gating effects of dopamine in dmPFC (Vander Weele et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vivo electrophysiology data in Figure 6, with a citation to prior work on dopamine in dmPFC.

claim: Dopamine has robust gating effects in dmPFC.
source: Although dmPFC neurons were responsive to photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, these responses did not appear to be dependent on the association between photostimulation with reward, despite the robust gating effects of dopamine in dmPFC (Vander Weele et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Cholinergic activity can itself become conditioned.
source: Rather than changing how other stimuli are processed from neutral into conditioned stimuli, our results suggest that cholinergic activity can itself become conditioned.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings that photostimulation can promote conditioned responding.

claim: Photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons during Photostim-Unreinforced sessions did not promote conditioned responding.
source: However, photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons during Photostim-Unreinforced sessions did not promote conditioned responding in these sessions, as might be predicted by a number of alternative interpretations, such as nonspecific increases in movement, arousal, or contextual awareness.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Photostimulated release of ACh can have a similar function as conditioned stimuli or cues, able to trigger conditioned responses.
source: Our findings suggest that photostimulated release of ACh can have a similar function as conditioned stimuli or cues, able to trigger conditioned responses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings that photostimulation can promote conditioned responding when paired with reward.

claim: Recent work has shown that basal forebrain cholinergic neurons are active following presentation of conditioned stimuli.
source: Recent work has shown that basal forebrain cholinergic neurons are active following presentation of conditioned stimuli (Crouse et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2019; Sturgill et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Work in visual cortex has suggested that ACh may help link stimuli with the time of expected rewards.
source: Additionally, work in visual cortex has suggested that ACh may help link stimuli with the time of expected rewards (Chubykin et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Cholinergic neurons were consistently active at the times of conditioned responding, even in the absence of cues and rewards.
source: We also demonstrated, however, that cholinergic neurons were consistently active at the times of conditioned responding, even in the absence of cues and rewards.
evidence: This claim is supported by GCaMP photometry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cholinergic transients are poised to play a role in conditioned responding and serve to signal more than just a salient event promoting a response.
source: This suggests that cholinergic transients are poised to play a role in conditioned responding and serve to signal more than just a salient event promoting a response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GCaMP photometry findings in Figure 3.

claim: Blocking cholinergic muscarinic receptors impaired the ability of mice to respond even to conditioned tones.
source: Indeed, blocking cholinergic muscarinic receptors impaired the ability of mice to respond even to conditioned tones (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacology data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Inhibition of cholinergic terminals in the BLA prevented mice from expressing freezing behavior at the time of fear conditioning.
source: This is consistent with other studies in which inhibition of cholinergic terminals in the BLA prevented mice from expressing freezing behavior at the time of fear conditioning (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: When photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons has previously been noted to increase discriminability between stimuli, it appears to do this primarily by increasing conditioned responses to conditioned stimuli, rather than suppressing false alarms.
source: Interestingly, even when photostimulation of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons has previously been noted to increase discriminability between stimuli, it appears to do this primarily by increasing conditioned responses to conditioned stimuli, rather than suppressing false alarms (Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: In sustained attention tasks to report the presence of stimuli to collect rewards, photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons promotes conditioned responding as if cues are present, even in their absence.
source: Additionally, in sustained attention tasks to report the presence of stimuli to collect rewards, photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons promotes conditioned responding as if cues are present, even in their absence (Gritton et al., 2016), and immunotoxic lesions of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons lead to omissions of any response at all (McGaughy et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Immunotoxic lesions of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons lead to omissions of any response at all in sustained attention tasks.
source: Additionally, in sustained attention tasks to report the presence of stimuli to collect rewards, photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons promotes conditioned responding as if cues are present, even in their absence (Gritton et al., 2016), and immunotoxic lesions of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons lead to omissions of any response at all (McGaughy et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The responses of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons and ACh release within the BLA indicate that conditioned responses of licking are represented by cholinergic signaling even in the absence of conditioned stimuli or reward delivery.
source: The responses of cholinergic basal forebrain neurons (Figure 3) and ACh release within the BLA (Figures 4 and 5) indicate that conditioned responses of licking are represented by cholinergic signaling even in the absence of conditioned stimuli or reward delivery, reminiscent of signals seen in lateral hypothalamic (LH) neurons projecting to the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Nieh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GCaMP and ACh sensor data, with a comparison to prior work.

claim: LH-VTA neurons were capable of promoting compulsive sucrose seeking behavior.
source: While LH-VTA neurons were capable of promoting compulsive sucrose seeking behavior, we do not observe the same stereotyped motor sequences in cholinergic neurons as when disinhibiting VTA dopamine neurons via the LH-VTA pathway (Nieh et al., 2016), and the ability of cholinergic signaling to promote compulsivity begs further exploration.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: We do not observe the same stereotyped motor sequences in cholinergic neurons as when disinhibiting VTA dopamine neurons via the LH-VTA pathway.
source: While LH-VTA neurons were capable of promoting compulsive sucrose seeking behavior, we do not observe the same stereotyped motor sequences in cholinergic neurons as when disinhibiting VTA dopamine neurons via the LH-VTA pathway (Nieh et al., 2016), and the ability of cholinergic signaling to promote compulsivity begs further exploration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the current findings to prior work.

claim: Cholinergic neurons from the basal forebrain have different projections depend on their location in the basal forebrain.
source: Cholinergic neurons from the basal forebrain have different projections depend on their location in the basal forebrain (Zaborszky and Gyengesi, 2012), and even within regions may be physiologically heterogeneous (Laszlovszky et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Even within regions of the basal forebrain, cholinergic neurons may be physiologically heterogeneous.
source: Cholinergic neurons from the basal forebrain have different projections depend on their location in the basal forebrain (Zaborszky and Gyengesi, 2012), and even within regions may be physiologically heterogeneous (Laszlovszky et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Photostimulation of anterior basal forebrain cholinergic neurons projecting to the lateral hypothalamus suppresses appetite.
source: While photostimulation of anterior basal forebrain cholinergic neurons projecting to the lateral hypothalamus suppresses appetite (Herman et al., 2016), here, photostimulation of the more posterior cholinergic population in the sublenticular substantia innominata/extended amygdala increased consummatory behavior (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Photostimulation of the more posterior cholinergic population in the sublenticular substantia innominata/extended amygdala increased consummatory behavior.
source: While photostimulation of anterior basal forebrain cholinergic neurons projecting to the lateral hypothalamus suppresses appetite (Herman et al., 2016), here, photostimulation of the more posterior cholinergic population in the sublenticular substantia innominata/extended amygdala increased consummatory behavior (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1.

claim: We did not observe an effect on locomotion, in both an unrewarded and a rewarded context, despite the physiological correlation of cholinergic neuron activity with locomotion.
source: We did not observe an effect on locomotion, in both an unrewarded and a rewarded context, despite the physiological correlation of cholinergic neuron activity with locomotion (Harrison et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current findings in the context of prior literature.

claim: Other work has suggested that photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic axonal terminals in the BLA can be rewarding.
source: Additionally, while other work has suggested that photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic axonal terminals in the BLA can be rewarding (Aitta-Aho et al., 2018), we did not observe a reinforcing effect of somatic basal forebrain cholinergic photostimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: We did not observe a reinforcing effect of somatic basal forebrain cholinergic photostimulation.
source: Additionally, while other work has suggested that photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic axonal terminals in the BLA can be rewarding (Aitta-Aho et al., 2018), we did not observe a reinforcing effect of somatic basal forebrain cholinergic photostimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4F.

claim: The more anterior portion of the basal forebrain, closer to the horizontal limb of the diagonal band of Broca (HDB), is more responsive to reward omission, more accurately classifies behavioral outcomes, and more closely tracks fluctuations in pupil-indexed global brain state.
source: This more anterior portion of the basal forebrain, closer to the horizontal limb of the diagonal band of Broca (HDB), is more responsive to reward omission, more accurately classifies behavioral outcomes, and more closely tracks fluctuations in pupil-indexed global brain state (Robert et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Cholinergic neurons in the more posterior portions of the basal forebrain are more responsive to unconditioned auditory stimuli, orofacial movements, aversive reinforcement, and showed robust associative plasticity for punishment-predicting cues.
source: In contrast, cholinergic neurons in the more posterior portions of the basal forebrain are more responsive to unconditioned auditory stimuli, orofacial movements, aversive reinforcement, and showed robust associative plasticity for punishment-predicting cues (Robert et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that project to the BLA develop earlier embryologically than those that project to cortex and hippocampus.
source: (1) basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that project to the BLA develop earlier embryologically than those that project to cortex and hippocampus (Allaway et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that project to the BLA rarely have collaterals.
source: (2) Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that project to the BLA rarely have collaterals (Carlsen et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that project to the BLA are sensitive to different immunotoxins and neurotoxins than cholinergic neurons that project to cortex and hippocampus.
source: (3) Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that project to the BLA are sensitive to different immunotoxins and neurotoxins than cholinergic neurons that project to cortex and hippocampus (Beninger et al., 2001; Boegman et al., 1992; Heckers et al., 1994; Hecker and Mesulam, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Backfiring from cholinergic axons in the BLA to the soma and then to cortex is likely to be limited.
source: This suggests that backfiring from cholinergic axons in the BLA to the soma and then to cortex is likely to be limited.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited evidence about the distinct nature of BLA-projecting cholinergic neurons.

claim: Heterogeneous responses among BLA neurons to photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons have been previously noted ex vivo.
source: We noted heterogeneous responses among BLA neurons in vivo to photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (Figure 6). Heterogeneous responses have also been previously noted ex vivo (Unal et al., 2015; Washburn and Moises, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Projecting, putative glutamatergic neurons were suppressed by cholinergic inputs.
source: Through a double transgenic approach, we determined that these heterogeneous responses could be explained on a cellular level, with projecting, putative glutamatergic neurons suppressed, and GABAergic, putative local interneurons neurons facilitated by cholinergic inputs (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7.

claim: GABAergic, putative local interneurons neurons were facilitated by cholinergic inputs.
source: Through a double transgenic approach, we determined that these heterogeneous responses could be explained on a cellular level, with projecting, putative glutamatergic neurons suppressed, and GABAergic, putative local interneurons neurons facilitated by cholinergic inputs (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The BLA GABAergic neuron population is thought to represent local interneurons that inhibit projection neurons.
source: The BLA GABAergic neuron population is thought to represent local interneurons that inhibit projection neurons (Washburn and Moises, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Both excitation of GABAergic neurons and inhibition of mPFC projection neurons were monosynaptic.
source: Although both excitation of GABAergic neurons and inhibition of mPFC projection neurons were monosynaptic, these cholinergic effects could in concert function to suppress BLA output (Lee and Kim, 2019; Pidoplichko et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2005), which may decouple regions downstream from the BLA, such as the dmPFC, and allow them to function independently with regard to cholinergic input or other inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7H and I.

claim: Cholinergic effects could in concert function to suppress BLA output.
source: Although both excitation of GABAergic neurons and inhibition of mPFC projection neurons were monosynaptic, these cholinergic effects could in concert function to suppress BLA output (Lee and Kim, 2019; Pidoplichko et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2005), which may decouple regions downstream from the BLA, such as the dmPFC, and allow them to function independently with regard to cholinergic input or other inputs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ex vivo findings, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Suppression of BLA output may decouple regions downstream from the BLA, such as the dmPFC, and allow them to function independently with regard to cholinergic input or other inputs.
source: Although both excitation of GABAergic neurons and inhibition of mPFC projection neurons were monosynaptic, these cholinergic effects could in concert function to suppress BLA output (Lee and Kim, 2019; Pidoplichko et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2005), which may decouple regions downstream from the BLA, such as the dmPFC, and allow them to function independently with regard to cholinergic input or other inputs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional consequences of BLA suppression.

claim: M1 muscarinic receptors are predominantly expressed by pyramidal neurons in the BLA.
source: Prior histological work had suggested that M1 muscarinic receptors are predominantly expressed by pyramidal neurons in the BLA (McDonald and Mascagni, 2010), and interneurons express nicotinic receptors (Pidoplichko et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Interneurons express nicotinic receptors.
source: Prior histological work had suggested that M1 muscarinic receptors are predominantly expressed by pyramidal neurons in the BLA (McDonald and Mascagni, 2010), and interneurons express nicotinic receptors (Pidoplichko et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Functional differences similar to those observed between excitatory and inhibitory neurons in the BLA have been seen in somatosensory cortex.
source: Functional differences similar to those we have observed between excitatory and inhibitory neurons have been seen in somatosensory cortex (Dasgupta et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The behavioral response to even brief photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons occurred by approximately 0.5 s.
source: Strikingly, the behavioral response to even brief photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons occurred by approximately 0.5 s (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The sub-second behavioral response appeared primarily mediated by slower muscarinic receptors rather than faster nicotinic receptors.
source: Surprisingly, this sub-second response appeared primarily mediated by slower muscarinic receptors rather than faster nicotinic receptors (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacology data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Augmenting cholinergic levels, even with temporal and spatial specificity through optogenetics, may have unpredictable effects depending upon the reward context surrounding this augmentation.
source: While there are many reasons that cholinergic augmentation is unlikely to treat any of these complex diseases completely, our translationally motivated concern is that augmenting cholinergic levels, even with temporal and spatial specificity here through optogenetics, may have unpredictable effects depending upon the reward context surrounding this augmentation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current findings about context-dependent effects of cholinergic stimulation.
